theme: Joint renewal, skill replacement, shared operations and dependencies
question: Can working services lack a feasible replacement trajectory, and how do shared deadlines, aging expertise and repair-based learning affect it under stated laws?
outcome: A frozen 36-state model enumerates 32 worlds, finite horizons and infinite sets. Budget 1 with aging skill permits three primary safe transitions without shocks, whereas nonaging skill permits indefinite survival. Budget 2 exceeds mean work 4/3 but cannot sustain state (1,1,1) indefinitely under separate costs. A post-baseline shared repair/training law enumerates 16 worlds and removes selected deficits: budget 1/no-shock and budget 2/all original supports become indefinitely viable from the primary state. Dependency cuts and seven accounting controls qualify provider counts and additional delivery.
challenge: Results depend on action costs, skill eligibility, shock severity, observation timing and the specified horizon. Technical selection does not establish distributed implementation, fairness, historical frequency or archaeological parameters.
remedy: Independent baseline reconstruction passes 5,218 checks; six counterexamples delimit broader implications. Reviewer severity and timing variants preserve the baseline. The separately frozen shared-operation law passes 1,133 reviewer checks and 1,968 independently written coordinator checks. Actual operations are counted once, with carried inventory and enactment conditions explicit.
retry_when: Independent historical or experimental evidence supports a changed wear, timing, learning-cost, supply or participation law. Preserve these endpoints; a new invented law should name the new premise and its test rather than imply archaeological calibration.
